paragraphs: A writer often longs more for the publicity and fame his writing brings than for the money he is paid. I was no exception. My heart burned. The next day I went to the producer and asked, "Why was my name not shown on the screen?" He replied, "Wait a little. Once you have publicity, I will put it in." The answer struck me as absurd. My eyes filled with tears. At once I decided to vacate the house and return to Tiruvarur with my wife.

My party friends in Coimbatore did not want me to leave. While I was there, I had been doing party work almost every day—meetings and speeches at the weddings of Kazhagam comrades. Navalar Nedunchezhiyan, then working as warden of a student hostel under the scientist G. D. Naidu, and I would walk five or six miles to take part in movement events. Once, with no transport from Coimbatore to a wedding at Kuniyamuthur, we bought groundnuts to munch and walked there and back.

Today, if there is a meeting at Chidambaram Park in Coimbatore, hundreds of thousands gather until the ground overflows. In those days our meetings were held in a tiny open space called Gandhi Square. If a thousand people came, it looked like five lakhs to us. How proud one feels looking back at the growth of the movement! Somehow I pacified my comrades and returned to Tiruvarur, without anxiety that I had quarrelled with a big film company, without fear of earning its displeasure, and without even thinking about what I would do next.

Film writing stopped. I wrote for journals and wrote plays. Devi Nataka Sabha was then camped in Tiruvarur. It had split from Sakthi Nataka Sabha, which itself had split from the famous Nawab Rajamanickam company. They asked me for a play. Taking Kundalakesi as the base and trying not to lose its literary richness, I wrote Manthiri Kumari. It was staged in Tiruvarur and then in Kumbakonam, where it became a great success.

I was invited to its silver-jubilee celebration. Padma came with me; she was pregnant then—yes, my eldest son Muthu lay quietly in her womb. After the performance many people gave speeches of praise, and I too had agreed to speak. Someone gave me a Kumbakonam betel beeda. I did not know its trick: a lump of lime had been placed inside for the eater to separate and spread in the needed amount. I put the whole thing into my mouth. The lime burned my mouth; saliva poured from my tongue, my tongue swelled, and I could not even close my mouth. How was I to make a thank-you speech? The felicitation ended without one.

I then planned to turn Murasoli, which I had been issuing as a leaflet, into a weekly from Tiruvarur. I pawned the jewellery in the house and started the weekly. It was printed at Karunanidhi Press in Tiruvarur, owned by Karunai Jamal. The paper was warmly received. Letters of praise piled up. But money from the sellers did not arrive.

Bringing out the weekly each week was like a surgical childbirth. The printer tolerated one week's debt, then two. By the third week he could not. What could he do? That was his position. We replaced the thali chain my wife wore with a simple thali cord, sold the chain, cleared two weeks of debt and took delivery of the third week's issue.

I could not afford either a worker or a vehicle to carry the copies from the press at Vijayapuram to the Tiruvarur office. The paper's manager Kanakasundaram and I would carry the bundles on our heads through the night. To cross the river there was a bamboo bridge. We carried the papers across it to the office, then sat up all night addressing and sending them to sellers and subscribers.

How long could a paper be run like this? Even as I fought over whether the paper would live or die, another great struggle began in my own life—the struggle to save my wife's life. Before that, however, came an unexpected political struggle.

India became independent in 1947. The long fire of liberation kindled by Lala Lajpat Rai, Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Gandhiji, Pandit Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Subhas Chandra Bose, Periyar, Thiru. Vi. Ka., V. O. Chidambaranar, Bharathi and countless tempered martyrs reached a decisive end. British rule granted India independence, and Jinnah, who had raised the demand for Pakistan, also achieved his goal.

Periyar issued a statement saying the day of Indian independence should be observed as a day of mourning. Arignar Anna replied that it was not a day of mourning but a day of joy. He argued firmly that one should not measure an event watched by the whole world solely by the yardstick of one's own doctrine; August 15 removed a two-century stigma and humiliation from the subcontinent and was therefore a festive day for the Dravidians as well. He answered Periyar's position line by line.

A deep split opened in the Dravidar Kazhagam. A major state conference was then arranged at Tuticorin, and Anna did not attend. The bitterness between Periyar and Anna increased. Some good people divided into two camps. Others who had not lifted even a straw for the party imagined they could use the quarrel to grow. Some demanded that Anna be expelled; in anger, a few even burned Anna's picture at the Tuticorin conference. When Anna heard all this, he smiled.

Wanting a bridge to be built between Periyar and Anna, I wrote a long article in the Murasoli weekly titled "The Last Days." I criticized the opportunists obstructing reconciliation. The article met fierce opposition within the Dravidar Kazhagam. Copies of Murasoli were burned in several places. Threatening letters arrived. Kazhagam members obstructed me from even getting the next issue printed.

It was in the middle of that party struggle that I had to enter the struggle to save my wife's life. The family prepared to take Padma to the hospital for childbirth. She had already had a mild fever for two days and was exhausted. A horse cart stood ready outside. Before she came into the street, they lit a kuthu-vilakku before the small shrine-box of Periya Thayar, the family deity worshipped in our house, and had her pray. Then they slowly brought her out. For some reason tears poured from her eyes. She noticed me watching her anxiously.
